speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to open debate on third reading of Bill C-165, an Act to provide for financial assistance for industrial development in all regions of Canada. Of course everyone in the House wants industrial development in all regions of Canada. I thank the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blen-karn) for letting me jump ahead of him in the line, so to speak, and open the debate, because I have other commitments later today. If I leave later, I do not want it to be seen as a discourtesy to the Hon. Member or to the Minister.
[DOT] (mo)
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) is present in the Chamber this morning. He has been here at every stage of the debate; he has answered all our questions. I must be careful in what I say because I do not want to give too much applause to the Minister, but I think it is fair to say that he has done quite a good job in getting the Bill through the House and in working with the Opposition on this important matter. I think it shows in the way the Bill has proceeded through the House.
I am a new person in the area of regional development. Previously I was energy critic, so this has opened my eyes somewhat and I have a little way to go. I want to make some comments on the Bill because I think it is really important for individual communities in Canada. It is not really that complicated when we get through all the letters, the little short forms, and so on. Basically it has some 17 Clauses. Like the majority of Government Bills these days, most of the job is done in the regulations over which we do not have control.
In general the Bill sets out a new system of awarding financial assistance for industrial and regional development. It works on what is a tier system, four tiers of arranging constituencies by census districts for qualification for grants. The Minister explained this in his speech. It is interesting because it is an attempt to bring together a number of government programs and put them into one program and make it what I think the Minister called a fast-tracking system, or a one-stop system, or whatever is the bureaucratic language, to indicate that it will make it easier for companies and individuals to apply for grants and financial assistance for economic development in Canada. Of course we are all in favour of that.
The problem with the Bill is really an old one, the problem of establishing an equitable system for giving grants. There has been much criticism of the old DREE program. I hesitate to use the word, because when I used "patronage" in committee, there were "oohs" and "ahs" as if patronage did not happen in Canada. Of course it does. The old system at least gave the aura of the possibility of patronage when the Minister really had to make decisions on pretty well his own criteria. That is simplifying matters, but this Bill tends to set out criteria. That is what I want to bring to the attention of the House.
We in the New Democratic Party are supporting the Bill. We are in favour of industrial and regional development. We would like to see the matter simplified and made less bureaucratic. We would like to see the system work a little fairer, and especially see it applied in a better way to the region where many of us have our seats, namely, western Canada. For those reasons we have tried to expedite passage of the Bill. However,

June 29, 1983
Industrial and Regional Development Act
we want to keep our eye on the Bill and on the system when it becomes law. I understand that it will be law by July 1. When I thought of all the work we were doing in committee, it made me laugh to think what would happen if we had changed things in committee; the forms might have to be changed and so on.
1 want to focus on the key to the Bill. It indicates that in order to obtain aid one has to fall into one of four tiers. One qualifies for more aid in Tier 4, a little less in Tier 3, and so on down to Tier 1. It is based upon a development index, which I think is the next part of the system. The index is based upon a per capita level of income, the level of employment in the district, and the capacity of the Province in which the district is located to raise revenue. As I stated before in committee, this is a problem for British Columbia because we have a higher per capita level of income. The average weekly wage in British Columbia is $464.15, as opposed to $341.66 in Newfoundland. We are more unionized. Our unions have forced good wages in British Columbia.
In many ways the tests that are in the Bill may make it more difficult for some regions to qualify in order to reach a higher tier, and, therefore, more aid. There is the term "capacity in the Province in which the district is located to raise revenues". Alberta has a Heritage Fund, and so on. I am told by the departmental officials, who have given me some papers, that they are trying to rationalize all these tests. I say that will be difficult. We will have a look at this Bill in about a year or so to see whether this development index is really working.
The Minister may not be aware of the kind of problems we have in my area of western Canada. I will just spend a couple of minutes on this. A headline in the Vancouver Sun for Thursday, June 23, 1983, reads, "Federal red tape the only product in Port Alberni". The article talks about the old ILAP program which applies to Port Alberni, as it is one of the designated areas. The article states there was to be a Christmas present of $15 million to the town. Six months later unemployment in that town is still running at 20 per cent, and the community leaders are still trying to unwrap the red tape in which the $15 million gift was wrapped. I believe they received only $1.4 million and only 133 low-paying jobs were created.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, ILAP is rolled into this Bill as one of the programs contained in it. It is very interesting, because the first paragraph in the newspaper article reads;
A federal Government program designed for the manufacturing East is not working among the woods of the West.
It shows the kind of problems we have in getting industrial development in different regions of Canada. Port Alberni on Vancouver Island is a beautiful place. It is a town dominated by MacMillan Bloedel, which is the main employer. The main employer is automating and putting technological change in its
plant. There are 2,000 fewer jobs than in April, 1981. That, together with the recession, has resulted in some real problems.
Many of the other jobs in the community come from servicing the main employer, the forestry industry. ILAP was supposed to be a program to help that area. However, instead of receiving $15 million, they received $1.4 million, which resulted in 133 temporary jobs with a pay rate of $175 per week, not exactly a booming pay rate.
It is interesting to see what is happening in the community. I use Port Alberni as one example in all the regional areas of Canada. The local Manpower manager there said that he has
2.400	people collecting unemployment insurance. There are
2,000	other people who have exhausted their unemployment benefits or are collecting social assistance, welfare. There are
1.400	others working part-time instead of full-time. This is out of a labour force of 13,000 people. It is typical of a lot of towns in the regional areas of Canada.
A business woman, Paula Anderson, was asked about this. She replied:
We cannot get manufacturing here. We are not in the Ontario heartland, we are on Vancouver Island and that has to be taken into consideration before it can have an impact on new industry. We want the program to be extended to primary industry.
That is part of the problem with this Bill. Let us look at the development index. The Minister was kind enough to have his officials give us a list of all the different ridings in which the tiers will apply. I have the list before me. When I look through it, I find it difficult to understand. I know that it is supposed to be fair, but I know that the Quebec constituency of Mount Royal is in Tier 2. Who represents that constituency, Mr. Speaker? The constituency of Saint-Henri-Westmount is in Tier 2. I am sure that this was done using an objective standard, but Regina East and Regina West are in Tier 1. Athabasca in northern Alberta is in Tier 1. In other words, these constituencies are in a less favoured category than are those two urban ridings in Montreal. Part of Comox-Powell River is in Tier 1.1 have never been there, but that is another area that is like Port Alberni. Port Alberni itself is in Tier 2.
The problem is that it is perceived, and it may be true, that the program will still benefit the manufacturing East and the central heartland more than it will benefit the regions. That is the problem that Port Alberni is faced with when it tries to develop. It is not a problem with an easy solution. How will industry be attracted to Port Alberni when it is really dependent on a resource based economy? Of course, that is part of the answer, but I just point out that some of these areas will not benefit as much as we hope they should.
It is interesting to note that in a Vancouver Sun interview of the Organization of Unemployed Workers-I have noticed that these organizations have grown up all over the country-a Mr. Brian Demorest was asked about ILAP and the programs for Port Alberni. He said that while the temporary jobs have
June 29, 1983

helped some people, as a family man he is better off on welfare. Then he said something very interesting. The article in the Sun reads:
He says he cannot see manufacturing industry of any size coming into town. Instead the OUW is calling for a six-hour working day (preferably at eight hours' pay but subject to negotiation) to be legislated throughout the province and the country.
This would create another shift and would take up some of the slack in unemployment.
Of course this is what the Government of France did as part of its industrial strategy. The Government of France, which these days has been much knocked, shortened working hours. This is probably what we will have to do in Canada, together with implementing programs for part-time work, and adopting other ways of coping with technological change.
1 am saying to the Minister that we are prepared to give the Bill a chance. We are prepared to pass it today, but we want to look a little more closely at these tiers. We appreciate that the Government is trying to be objective in the sense of a development index, but we wonder if development really can be attracted to the Port Alberni's of the country under this program.
There are three other comments I would like to make before I conclude. First, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kam-loops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), raised the matter of native employment, a matter which is very important in the West. The Minister answered the question, and I appreciate that, by saying that that matter is not really being dealt with under this Bill, as I understand it, but would be dealt with under another program. I note that answer.
The second matter I raise is that the Minister talked about decentralizing, and 1 am a little suspicious of this. I think that there is a lot of centralizing in this Bill, in the sense that the federal Government, because it has been burned by the Provinces, and the Provinces have taken credit for some of the things the federal Government put money into, is, as a political strategy, trying to do things more directly.
I am a little worried about the effect some of these programs might have on federal-provincial relations because 1 do believe deeply that co-operative federalism is the only way to make Canada work. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has failed absolutely in bringing some of the principles of co-operative federalism to the West.

speechtext:
The Hon. Member pooh-poohs that statement, but he is not the one who gave the Salmon Arm situation in the interior of British Columbia to the people out there.
There are other problems with the program that we would want to examine. There are certainly some questions about some of the Government guarantees that have been picked up in this Bill, such as guarantees to Canadair, Maislin, and other companies. Canadair is a Crown corporation in need of reform. Some of the other programs smell a little of the
Industrial and Regional Development Act
corporate welfare that has been handed out fairly indiscriminately, but I will give the Minister the benefit of the doubt on that score. I think he is really trying, and he believes in industrial development. He is from Cornwall, a small town, and I think he is concerned with getting industrial development established.
We cannot have this policy in isolation, Mr. Speaker. We need an industrial strategy for Canada. The example that I used of Port Alberni brings out the fact that there are areas with primary industry only, and no manufacturing base around it. Manufacturing still takes place in the heartland of the country, and that is a real problem for the West and the Maritimes. So much of our industry is foreign owned and controlled that, as well as a regional development strategy, I think we need a whole new Canadian development strategy.
In January a press release was issued about the reorganization of the Minister's Department, Bill C-152. It was accompanied by a big wad of briefing papers which showed it was based on an industrial strategy which was a spin-off from megaprojects. That strategy has gone by the board and the Government has admitted that, so it is looking for another industrial strategy but so far it has not found one.
In subsequent speeches in the House on industrial development I will suggest that the industrial strategy be based on a regional stance and ways of upgrading the regions by means better than those set out in this Bill.
I know the Hon. Member for Mississauga South has a much more detailed mind than I have, and he knows this area very well. Tom Axworthy, the Prime Minister's principal secretary, was talking about these Government development programs and he said that we want to move in on the West like the little bird that sits behind the elephant's ear. I can tell him, Mr. Speaker, that he will find that it is like the elephant who danced among the chickens and said, "Let's make it fair- every man for himself." As a chicken, he is going to have a problem among all those western elephants.
The New Democratic Party supports the Bill, Mr. Speaker, but we have concerns about whether it is going to reach the Port Alberni's of the country. I look forward to the Bill's record receiving committee examination about a year from now. We will find out then if we have really made progress in something that every Member of the House wants, and that is regional industrial development. We must have a fair system all across the country from which everyone can benefit in this great country with the industrial system that we have.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with third reading of Bill C-165. I want to say at the outset that while this Bill does not go in the direction that this Party would go in dealing with industrial development of the regions of Canada, particularly those that are disadvantaged, it is an improvement on what has been happening, and so we support it fully.

June 29, 1983
Industrial and Regional Development Act
I was very pleased with the way the Minister responded yesterday in committee, accepting w'hat we feel were important amendments to define the eligibility of persons entitled to apply. The report on the IRD program will be made immediately after June 1 each year, so that when we determine the new tier levels on July 1, Members on the Committee for Industrial and Regional Development will be able to make some contribution suggesting how the program might be altered in the ensuing year.
The Minister was quite responsive to the sunset clause. This is the kind of legislation that should always contain sunset clauses. It is a grant contribution guarantee type program administered by the Government, in an effort to solve a problem. It may not solve the problem however. It is certainly not a permanent solution to anything. I think the Minister would agree that it is a temporary effort to get at a headache, and that the remedy for that headache should be reviewed from time to time. The sunset for this legislation is five years. In our view that is an important clause, and I thank the Government for accepting our suggestion and amending the Bill in that respect.
This Bill has one other advantage in that it stops some of the alphabet soup. The Bill is intended to replace the EDP, the I LAP, RDIA and the STEP programs. Therefore we now have IRD replacing EDP, ILAP, RDIA and STEP. Unfortunately, there are still five other programs. They are SERB, SAP, IERD, SPLA, and the FDBD.
It is about time that the various programs of the Government were amalgamated, in the sense that this Bill amalgamates programs, puts the bureaucracy which manages programs under one roof, reduces that bureaucracy, makes sure that individual bureaucracies are not competing one with another, and makes it easier for the business community, who may want to apply for the grants, loans, contributions or what have you, which may be available under this program. They at least have one-stop shopping, certainly for the four items which are amalgamated under the new IRD Program.
We would not have proceeded this way. First of all we believe that it is most difficult, well nigh impossible, for people in the Public Service to understand properly the motivations which inspire people to build plants, create new jobs, create new wealth, the motivations which put new people to work on new programs and new projects. The entrepreneur works on the basis of hopes and dreams. He thinks on the basis not of what the steak looks like, but what sizzle, sound and smell are in terms of profit, gain or reward. It is difficult to put that type of thinking into a brief and have that brief examined by unseen and unknown persons in a Government office, and somehow come up with something which really makes the country grow.
What we would have done, therefore, would have been to turn the matter over to the tax system. As we proposed in the last election, we would have a tax credit scheme. In areas which are depressed, where there are no jobs, and where there needs to be development, we would say to the investor who goes into those areas that not only can he get his money back
completely before he pays a nickel in taxes, but he can get 150 per cent or even 200 per cent back before he pays a nickel in taxes.
He still has to put his money, his ambition and desires up front, because we say, "We are giving you the carrot, the carrot of an opportunity to make a profit. It is not a cheap loan, not a guarantee and not some sort of percentage contribution based on some mythical unemployment rate in your community or lack of development in your community. It is an opportunity to make a profit, to put your money up. And you will really make a profit on that basis if you go into a depressed area, because when you invest in that depressed area you will be able to get your money back, perhaps even doubled, without the tax man taxing you." That is the opportunity. That is the sizzle. That is the drive. That is the offer.
What do we have here? We have money coming up front, albeit, but coming from a bureaucracy which really has no way of properly judging the spirit, the entrepreneurship, those subjective things which make one person a super businessman and another person a failure. Business is that way. All of the education, all of the training, all of the work which go into a business where you might say on paper the credentials look good, do not really matter. What we are really talking about is that inner spirit which makes some people succeed in business, an inner spirit which makes some people grow and go, and gives some people the ability to put their neighbours to work, to build a country. But some people have not got it.
The problem with the system whereby we have those in the bureaucracy judging applications, is that there is no way in which they can put on paper or justify in a committee meeting that inner spirit which makes success a possibility. So we say, get the Government out of it. Get the Government out of it, but leave the big carrot there. If you really want to build an area which does not have much going for it, put the carrot there, the tax carrot, the allowance. Give these people the ability to make a real profit, because that is what makes our system grow and go in the market place. That is what motivates people. People are not motivated for altruistic reasons. They do not work day and night for altruistic reasons. They go out and work because they want to build for themselves and their families, and because they want to get ahead, and if you offer to them a better opportunity to get ahead in one place in the country than in another, they will go to that place where they have the best opportunity.
One other problem with this piece of legislation is that I, personally, am afraid that in spreading the wealth in terms of the money which is available for Government assistance to business across the entire country, we may have inadvertently-and I give this as a word of caution to the Minister and the Government-hurt some of those areas-the Alberni's of which my friend was talking-in terms of their ability to grow and go. Because what has been done is to make it possible for every area in Canada to get some form of Government assistance in terms of a loan, a grant, a contribution, or in terms of a guarantee of some kind.
June 29, 1983

Mississauga will get assistance in the same way as Cape Breton. You might be able to get more assistance in Cape Breton, but you can still get assistance in Mississauga. As an Hon. Member from Mississauga I have no objection to that. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid), who is in the same position, also has no objection to that. However, I would like to say this to you, Sir, and to the Minister, that there is only so much money, and I suggest that the Minister and his officials are looking for success. If they can back a project in an area where success is likely, they will back it there. It is sometimes easier to back a project in Brampton or Mississauga than it is in Cape Breton. Statistically, the chance of success may well be far higher in Brampton or Mississauga than it is in Cape Breton.
[DOT] (M40)
The Minister is likely to see a situation where his officials will find applications coming from some of the top Tier 1 areas which are very likely to succeed and will make the officials in the Department look good. Those applications are likely to take up the money. Applications from areas in the country where the chance of success is not near as great are not likely to get as much money as they might ordinarily get, because again there is only so much in the till.
1 am not saying we are opposing the Bill. We think it is good and should go through. While 1 suspect that the Minister, even though he is a pretty good one, is not going to be a Minister of the Crown very much longer-the people of Canada are going to make sure that he and his colleagues find some other place to work, and perhaps they will need the advantage of some of these programs-I say to the Minister that in his management of the Department he had better be very careful to make sure that the limited money available is used to get rid of some of the existing inequities and disparities in this country as opposed to the politically and bureaucracy pleasing support of propositions from areas where the success rate is very likely to be much higher.
I will now deal with the question of tiering, Mr. Speaker. For the purposes of this Bill the country is divided into tier areas. Tier 1 covers a good part of the country; most of the major cities are tier 1 or, at the worst Tier 2. Then there is a whole series of criteria which determine Tier 2, Tier 3 or Tier 4 areas. One of the concerns I have with the Bill and the proposed regulations is the contribution the Government can make to a project. It is higher in Tier 4 than in Tier 3 or 2 or 1, and the level at which the program kicks in is lower in Tier 4, 3 and 2, than it is in 1. But the effect is to have virtually the same element of subsidization in all four tier areas.
For example, if the Government is going to give a contribution to marketing of a manufacturer's product in the Tier 1 zone, it could go up to 50 per cent of the cost. But even in Tier 4 zones the maximum is 75 per cent. Bearing in mind that the Tier 4 zones are the areas of the worst unemployment, the worst possible disparity in the country, and bearing in mind that the Tier 1 zones are the most prosperous areas in the
Industrial and Regional Development Act
country, the variance is between 50 per cent and 75 per cent. I say to you, Sir, that is not much of a variance.
Perhaps the Minister might take a look at that because, while I know he wants to make sure his Department is dealing right across Canada and that there is no discrimination in the country, the whole nature of regional economic development is that we discriminate in the less developed, less prosperous parts of the country. The concept is that you help a person in a weak area more than you help a person in a wealthy area. But the regulations do not clearly make it less attractive in a wealthier area. To put it the other way, you put just about as many bucks in Mississauga as you do in Cape Breton. If that is really the intention, and I suspect it is not, then perhaps there should be some change in the proposed regulations.
As I said previously, we would not have proceeded this way, but we are pleased to support this Bill because we believe it is progressive and a better way of handling the problems than we have had so far from this Government. On that basis 1 commend the Minister for being prepared to accept amendments and allowing the Members in committee to make valid input to the legislation. If we had that type of co-operation from other Ministers, for example the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) on the Export Development Corporation Bill, that Bill could move ahead too. But when we have a Government Department which stonewalls the Opposition and any effective and proper suggestions, then you do not get matters moving ahead in this Parliament. This Minister is cooperative. The Bill was introduced about a week ago; hopefully it can pass today before noon.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; Minister of Regional Economic Expansion

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to thank my colleagues on both sides of the House for allowing me the opportunity to wrap up third reading of this Bill on behalf of the Government. I also want to pay tribute to the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), and the Official Opposition critic, the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie), for their constructive criticism and comments with respect to regional development, in the Standing Committee on Regional Development from whence came a lot of the ideas incorporated in this Bill.
I want to address a couple of the issues, Mr. Speaker, that the two Hon. Member have raised today, as well as a brief summary of the Bill. Members of Parliament are all busy these days in committees as well as carrying out our responsibilities to our individual ridings that I think it will take a while before

June 29. 1983
Industrial and Regional Development Act
the full impact of this Bill is realized by all Members of this House, and particularly how it affects all parts of the country. This is the first time in almost 15 years, since the Department of Regional Expansion was initiated, that the Department has gone through a thorough re-evaluation and reorientation of its regional development programs.
I think it speaks well of Parliamentarians in general that, of all, the three Parties support the Bill. That has not happened too often during this particular Parliament. Second, there was the non-partisanship. I have been on the Committee on Regional Development for eight or nine years. I also happened to be chairman of the Committee at one time when I first came to the House. I think that non-partisanship is attributable to the importance that each and every Hon. Member, regardless of his or her political persuasion, attaches to regional development.
I would like to summarize some of the most important parts of the Bill. For the first time in Canada's history we will have a consistent measure to gauge regional disparity in Canada. The arbitrariness of the Minister of the day or of the Government of the day deciding which area of the country receives what level of assistance with respect to industrial restructuring and regional development, is past.
We have spent a great deal of time in putting the development index together. 1 appreciate the constructive input we have had from Hon. Members on ail sides of the House, from the private sector, and from provincial Governments, with respect to the development of this index. It is not perfect. I doubt very much if there is such a thing as a perfect development index. However, I think that we are well along the way toward developing an index which, as the Hon. Member said in their second reading speeches and in committee, is as equitable, as objective, and as fair as any that has ever been previously developed.
I would like to address the second most important part of the program. It is no longer a question as to whether one particular area is designated or not. It is now a question of degree of designation. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South said that he could receive almost the same assistance for Mississauga as one can receive for Cape Breton. On the contrary. If one looks, for example, to the most important part of the regional development, in other words, the basic program element upon which DREE was originally initiated or founded, one finds that it was the establishment of new industries, the diversification of the economic base of the regional disparity areas in Canada. One sees that in areas in the most developed 50 per cent of the country, unless their unemployment population ratio exceed by 1 per cent the national average for six consecutive months, there is no financial assistance from the Government of Canada for new establishments. Yet in the Tier IV areas, those companies applying for assistance to start new ventures are eligible for up to 60 per cent of capital costs to undertake these ventures.
Forgetting for a second southern Ontario, or the southern part of British Columbia, but take a Province like Nova Scotia, one finds that it was very difficult to try to develop certain areas like Cape Breton when the same financial assistance was applicable to companies in the Halifax area. Now there is a differentiation even within individual regions. You will know, Mr. Speaker, that there are substantial degrees of economic disparity within your own particular Province. Now that we have a consistent measure for regional disparity, it will be much easier to differentiate between those various areas.
The other comment of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, and I think it was a justifiable one, concerned success. What our officials are after is success in terms of the number of jobs we will create in every region of the country as a result of the program. We are quite prepared to take a much higher risk for projects in the more disadvantaged areas of Canada than we are in the most developed regions.
The third element that I consider to be so important with respect to the Bill is that, for the first time, we have a manageable number of programs that can now be delivered on a regional basis. With my background as a small and mediumsized entrepreneur and as a mayor of a community which once had the highest unemployment rate in Canada, I have always felt that if one really wants to reach out, if one really wants to solve regional disparity, one must bring all the economic tools of Government to bear. It does not just require one program or two programs. It requires all the programs. From now on, all the economic development programs, the direct delivery programs of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, will be available in every region of the country.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway spoke of the Port Alberni's of this world, the single industry regions, and of the difficulties that one faces in trying to diversify the economic base of those regions that are resource-based and so dependent on one single industry. One of the elements by which the Bill will facilitate in the diversification of the economic base in these areas is through regionalizing the financial assistance for innovation such as design, research and development, et cetera. In other words, we will try to encourage more of these single industry communities to carry out more research and development, to expand their product lines or expand their processing. This is one of the avenues that has really not been addressed to any degree in terms of regional development potential for the past 15 or 20 years.
The other element mentioned by the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway was decentralization. This really is decentralization. I think the previous concept of decentralization was sharing the responsibility with the Provinces.That is just one element and we will still do that with the general development subagreements with the Provinces. However, I think the key with this program is that we not only decentralize the delivery mechanism to reach out to the small and medium-sized entrepreneur in every region of the country, but we also decentralize the processing of the applications so that
June 29, 1983

there is a regional perspective in the assessment of the individual applications.
If we were preparing a headline, in the creating of a PR program to promote the program, I would say to every small and medium sized entrepreneur, "You no longer have to come to Ottawa for financial assistance. We will reach out to you". We will ensure that the small and medium-sized entrepreneurs in Canada, who obviously make up the backbone of economic development in Canada, will receive their fair share of all the programs which have historically only been available to most of the major corporations in the most developed regions of the country.
I also want to pay tribute to my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane), the Hon. Member for Matapedia-Matane who, for two and one-half years, was the Minister responsible for DREE before the reorganization. Since the inception of DREE, he is really the first Minister I have known, and I think I have known them all, who has really tried to address the issue in the most sensitive way, the issue of regional development. Many of the provisions that are incorporated in the Bill I was able to obtain from his previous work in this regard.
The other element of the Bill which we have not discussed to any degree concerns industrial restructuring. If there is one message that came home to me loud and clear during the two and one half years 1 spent as Trade Minister, in travelling to over 50 countries around the world, was the fact that the competition Canadian industry will face over the balance of this decade and of this century will be tougher than we have ever faced before. Therefore, that tells each and every one of us, regardless of our position, that our industries will have to maintain their international competitiveness. That is an undeniable fact. If we are not competitive, we will not survive economically. If we do not survive, not only will we not create the new jobs that are necessary in Canada, but we will not maintain the ones we already have, either.
This industrial restructuring element of the program is as equally important as the regional development priority of the program. That is the reason why we think it is so important to have this national program sensitized on a regional basis. Even in the industrial heartland of Canada there are a number of industries that need financial assistance from the Government to undertake expansion programs, modernization programs or innovation programs to ensure that their companies will be internationally competitive. I believe it was the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway who probably expressed it best on behalf of all of us in the House the other day on second reading when he said, "What is in this Bill is almost too good to be true . I think that is really one of the reasons we have not truly digested its contents, the fact that for one of the few occasions when we have a program in which all Members of Parliament have had some input.
I welcome the amendments brought forward by the Opposition. I think that together, we should not wait until the end of the year when the program will be reviewed. Yesterday, I
Industrial and Regional Development Act
made a commitment to the committee that any changes in the regulations would be brought to the committee's attention. I believe that the more input we have in this particular area, the better the program will be.
In conclusion, perhaps the best indication that we have done something constructive and positive as Parliamentarians is the fact that we have received no press coverage with respect to the program. That is usually the best indication that we have done something constructive and positive. If the Opposition would have stonewalled the Bill or objected to it, this legislation would probably have been on the front page of every paper in the country and the First story on television and radio news. But the fact of the matter is that we have all agreed on a program which provides financial assistance of anywhere from $500 million to $1 billion a year to manufacturing, processing, tourism and related service sector industries right across the country. Since we have received no publicity, it is probably the best indication that we are on the right track.
1 also want to thank my provincial colleagues. I discussed this particular program with my provincial colleagues even before it was passed through the Cabinet. I think their input into this Bill has been very important.
At a time when some 1.5 million Canadians are unemployed, I do not think there is any Member of the House who would not agree that a concerted effort is needed toward strengthening our industries. I do not think any Member of Parliament, regardless of his or her political persuasion, will rest easy until such time as we have full employment in this country.
In my trade days, we had a very cohesive effort between the private and public sectors, whether it was management, labour, federal or provincial Governments. There was a very co-operative effort. I suggest that is one reason why Canadian exports were able to not only maintain but increase their market share and Canada was one of the few countries in the world to achieve this goal during the international recession of the last three years.
I feel very strongly that if we are to be successful with this program, solve the problems of regional disparity and industrial restructuring and create the needed jobs that we want in this country, we will need that cohesive effort by management and labour, the federal, provincial and municipal Governments. I think Members on both sides of the House have demonstrated that co-operation in their input into this program, and as Minister responsible I want to say thank you to each individual.

subtopic: ATHLETIC CONTESTS AND EVENTS POOLS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GOVERNMENT OPERATED POOL SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this third and perhaps last opportunity to put some final comments on the record with respect to Bill C-95. Needless to say, as I have said so many times before, I view the impending passage of this legislation with mixed emotions. On the one hand it is an abysmally bad piece of legislation. I am positive, and the Opposition is just as assured, that it will return to haunt the House at a later time. Yet I am left with the feeling that because of the great amount of public relations expended in Government advertising, there is the possibility that at least some of the beneficiaries named in this Bill may reap some benefit.
We on this side can take some pride in our efforts to improve the Bill. I refer to the amendments which we raised in committee and discussed very briefly earlier this week. I will comment on those shortly, but before I make those comments,
I want to point out some of the existing conflicts and pressures which exist in the House at this time.
Against those conflicts there is one prevailing matter that seems to have been raised consistently by the Government side. It is the obvious, outspoken, obnoxious desire of the federal Government to get back into the lottery business. We have opposed this re-entry of the federal Government into the lottery business from the very start. No individual, group or Province can fault the efforts and sincerity of a great number of our Members who have presented their arguments in the House in opposition to the re-entry of the federal Government into the gaming business.
Our difficulties with Bill C-95 are deeply rooted and have been long lasting. It would be only appropriate to review the record and set matters straight after a lengthy and controversial exchange.
In 1976, our Party had to make a very difficult decision with respect to Loto Canada. The Montreal Olympics had incurred a deficit of approximately $1 billion and the federal Government was pressured by Montreal to get it out of the quagmire in which it found itself. The federal Government promised to assist in the reduction of that $1 billion deficit which Montreal faced.
That was a fair and perhaps reasonable undertaking by the federal Government because the Montreal Olympic Games were a source of pride not only for the people of Montreal and the Province of Quebec but for all Canadians as we reflected in the glory and success of the Montreal Olympics. It was an event which Canadians of all ages and from every region enjoyed and participated in in whatever way possible. It was an event of national and international significance.
As is the case today, the Liberal Government of 1976 was short of cash. Therefore it insisted that whatever help it gave to Montreal would have to be met by non-government revenues, so it said. Therefore the federal Government introduced a federal lottery. For many good reasons, the Opposition of the day was opposed to the introduction of Loto Canada. First, it was said that lotteries were a matter of provincial jurisdiction. But notwithstanding our objection, the federal Government remained adamant; it was Loto Canada or nothing.
In committee we extracted a promise from the federal Government, and particularly the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), that Loto Canada would have a fixed three-year term and would be conducted primarily for the benefit of the Montreal Olympics. The present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources made a great show of his distaste for lotteries and of his desire to help Montreal. The same Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was full of enthusiasm at the prospect of being able to turn lotteries back to the Provinces at the end of that three-year term.
On the strength of the Minister's comments, the Progressive Conservative Party voted in favour of supporting Loto Canada. Our support was not for Loto Canada or any other lottery, bookie operation or gambling racket, but for a Canadian city hosting the Summer Olympic Games. That is why, with respect to the sports pool, we as a Party support the allocation of federal funds to the City of Calgary so that it might adequately host the XV Winter Olympic Games.
All Hon. Members know the story of Loto Canada and how scandal-ridden its life was. Everyone knows how the Loto Canada corporation with all its hangers on became the haven of patronage, resulting in much mismanagement and many misdemeanours. My colleagues the Hon. Member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski) and the Hon. Member for Bramp-ton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) spelled out some of these disreputable and disgraceful instances in the debate earlier this week. Loto Canada was one of the greatest pork barrels of all time.
Despite that record and despite the present Minister of Energy's assurances given in 1976, the 1979 Liberal Government proposed that Loto Canada be continued in perpetuity. I would have thought that any government with any reasonable ounce of conscience would have said that it had had enough of Loto Canada's reputation hanging around its neck as it faced an election. The extension of Loto Canada's life, Mr. Speaker, was something totally unacceptable to our Party.
The long and the short of the matter is that the federal Government has no business in the lottery or the gaming business. While the tendency of the Liberals is to hide issues at election time, we campaigned as a Party right across the nation during the 1979 election compaign to put an end to the sorry chapter of the Liberal Government's participation in the gaming business. There was no equivocation in our position, and it was a campaign promise that we kept.
June 29, 1983

The sale of Loto Canada remains controversial simply because too many people, including the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan), just simply refuse to look at the facts. Loto Canada was not the success that government advertising leads the people of Canada to believe. The facts show very clearly that there was a decline in returns over the years of its operation. Loto Canada's very best year was 197778 when it netted $74.3 million. But by the following year that net had declined to $62.5 million, and even if Loto Canada had had a full year of operation in 1979-80, it would not have netted $62.5 million. Loto Canada was, therefore, clearly in decline.
These facts notwithstanding, we still hear the Minister of State for International Trade talking about Loto Canada yielding $80 million to $100 million a year in revenue.

speechtext: Net.

subtopic: ATHLETIC CONTESTS AND EVENTS POOLS ACT

speechtext:
That is right, net. Where will the Minister gain the revenue of $300 million to return that $80 million to $100 million in net profits or gains to the beneficiaries as enunciated in this Bill? The Minister in his heart knows better. He knows that the sports pool is doomed to failure. The only salvation he will have is that if he gets back into the lottery business then we will be back in competition with the Provinces as we were before. We will be back in competition in the news media. Each one will be vying for the same thing with an expenditure of dollars, the likes of which we have never seen. Even though Loto Canada was once known as the greatest advertising spender in the whole country, that will be nothing to what it will be if Loto Canada gets back into the games business.
The 1979 Progressive Conservative Government had a difficult time disposing of a failing product, an asset that was declining in value almost daily but certainly monthly. My colleague from Edmonton North went into some detail on Monday night explaining the results of that sale and the benefit to this country of that sale. Not only did the Hon. Member get a good deal for the Government of the day, but he provided a fixed annual return for arts and culture and fitness and amateur sport. As at the end of this month the federal Government will have received approximately $102.5 million from the Provinces pursuant to the 1979 agreement.
Again, the Minister of State for International Trade chooses to ignore the facts and mocks the value of that agreement. Show me any deal in which the federal Government can get over $32 million a year at absolutely no cost, Mr. Speaker, and I will show you a deal that we should grab and grab quickly. After all, we are talking about the need to fulfil a commitment of $200 million from non-tax revenue for the 1988 Calgary Olympics when that 1979 agreement would have solved the problem.
Between 1983 and 1988, assuming 6 per cent inflation, the Provinces will have paid to this Government $220 million. Why could that money not have been used to fund the Calgary games so the organizers could have in advance adequately planned a successful games venture? Unfortunately, the federal Government has seen fit to spend the money from the lottery agreement on other items. The federal Government
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
says that fitness and amateur sport and arts and culture are getting increased benefits through the ordinary budget system. But no one knows for sure because the money from that 1979 lottery agreement goes into the Consolidated Revenue Fund. The Government has not been able to explain that away, either in committee or during Question Period.
However, the important factor in all of this is that the federal Government has a binding agreement with the Provinces not to re-enter the lottery field. This Government may miss the good old patronage days, but that is too bad. Bill C-95 is nothing more than an end run around the 1979 federal-provincial agreement.
I opened my remarks by saying that the legislation before us is bad. It is worse than that, Mr. Speaker. In committee and earlier this week we tried to improve upon it. First, I know of no other country in the world which distinguishes in the gaming business between a lottery and a sports pool.
Second, there may not be a court in the land-and this was tested in one of the Provinces already-that will see a difference between the federal Government's re-entry into the sports pool and a re-entry into the lottery or gaming business.
Third, the legislation, as contained in Bill C-95, provides a Mack truck clause because it contains a simple clause that allows the federal Government to get back into any other lawful game. Once this Bill is passed, who knows what kind of a game the Government will become involved in, because the legislation will permit the Government to become involved in any kind of a game. The Government will be able to legalize any game, as it has this one. It is make it illegal for anybody else to play in that game but the Government of Canada. It will be the sole gambler and the sole host of a gambling nest of games-lottery games, sports, pools, video tape games, electronic games, even perhaps an electronic game of chess and you will be betting against yourself.
Fourth, Bill C-95 makes it possible for this to happen and lists every beneficiary known to the Minister of State for International Trade without honouring a commitment to any one of them, including the Calgary Olympics, because the Bill does not make any allocation of funds among those beneficiaries with any degree of certainty, by percentage or otherwise.
Fifth, the proposed sports pool corporation will not be subject to the kind of scrutiny and audit demanded by Canadians. We are sick and tired of Crown corporations running wild. The Auditor General has pointed out that Crown corporations are almost a sub-parliamentary group subject to a little bit of accountability to none at all. And here we are talking about establishing a new Crown corporation dealing with the games business. As we mentioned yesterday, the odds against Canadians participating in this game is bad enough without their being subjected to the abuse and error they were earlier with Loto Canada. That should not happen again. We should attempt to protect Canadians by having the Auditor General audit the books of the corporation and set up the appropriate systems.

June 29, 1983
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
The Government has refused to table any marketing studies to indicate that sports pools are saleable or marketable. On the other hand, the Provinces have provided to date the only facts and figures relating to sports pools. They indicated very clearly in committee that the game is doomed to failure and that we are about to lose our shirts by entering into competition with the Provinces.
Bill C-95 is ostensibly all about the aggressive marketing of a federal sports pool, yet it provides the sports pool corporation with a start-up grant of SI0.5 million to run a gambling business and a line of credit of an additional $20 million, with no obligation on its part to repay those advances of taxpayers' money. If the Government is so sure of success in the sports pool game, why does it not make provision for repayment of the start-up funds provided by the taxpayers of the nation to the corporation? It could make repayment from its revenues, especially if the Government is sure that the sports pool will be successful. No ordinary Canadian wanting to open a business could get a deal like that one.
The Government has still not responded to the points made by the Inter-Church Committee on Lotteries as to the detrimental effect Bill C-95 will have on our society. The Committee pointed out that the games business, including lotteries, is the greatest social disease of our time. I am sure Hon. Members of the House and the public have read recently about the addiction of certain persons, for example the $175,000 which was stolen by a bank teller because of her desire to continue to buy tickets. At one time the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Fleming) were both vocal in their opposition to lotteries, but neither saw fit to raise those concerns during the debate on Bill C-95. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) saw fit not to speak in a debate despite, as she said, her loathing for such activity.
Finally, Bill C-95 will contribute to the steadily deteriorating relationship between the federal and provincial Governments. No effort was made by the federal Government to discuss what arrangements could be made with the Provinces to assist in the Financing of the Calgary Olympics, and the Mack truck clause mentioned earlier is nothing short of a red flag to the Provinces because they view it as a deliberate attempt by the federal Government to get back into the lottery business in competition with them.
The position of the Progressive Conservative Party on the subject of federal involvement in the games, lottery and gambling field is clear and unequivocal. We are opposed to the re-entry of the federal Government into the gambling business. Our opposition is made much easier in the context of Bill C-95 because it is a bad, ill-conceived Bill. There will be no end to the controversy, and I suspect the Government will have its hands full trying to account for this new Crown corporation, just as it had its hands full with Loto Canada. Had our amendments concerning the Auditor General and the elimination of the Mack truck clause been accepted, it might have been a
little easier and perhaps more beneficial to the Government. Nonetheless, democracy must take its course, but to what end?
There is only so much an opposition can do to save a government from its own folly. I am extremely appreciative of the support and concern shown by my colleagues and their participation in the debate. I thank them publicly for their participation and for echoing their concerns, just as I have echoed mine. Having fought the fight, the good fight, I naturally want to wish the sports pool corporation well. I trust the Calgary Olympics, the Winter Olympics, will soon benefit from whatever game the Government proposes to introduce. To that end I have to allow that modest acceptance of the position now taken by the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I hear the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid). It is not a matter of "finally"; it has nothing to do with that. It is that we stated our unequivocal opposition to the Bill on second reading. I think our position on balance is somewhat clearer than the position of the Conservative Party inasmuch as it is not a structural opposition to the nature of the Bill in terms of the way it has been drafted, whether it has been drafted well or otherwise. Our opposition is not simply to the federal Government's participation. It is not an opposition which indicates that somehow or other the federal Government opted out of the lottery business and therefore to opt back in would be wrong. Our opposition is that we are opposed to lotteries of this type and to further institutionalizing gambling in this way.
There are sufficient opportunities for people to engage in games of chance all across the country without adding to the number. I am as convinced of that as was the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) some years ago when he spoke similarly on the introduction of lotteries and gambling. I am as convinced today as I was many years ago when I was in the Legislature of the Province of Ontario that the introduction of gambling turns out to be a tax on the poor and to be more attractive to those people of very limited means than it is to those of considerable wealth. The chance of victory, of winning fabulous wealth, is remote. "Remote" hardly describes it: "virtually non-existent" might better describe the situation. The chance of victory is a lure which people of little income find almost irresistible. I believe the Government does the country a disservice by introducing at this point in time the particular proposal for a sports pool.
I have listened with interest over the course of the last few days, in fact at every turn when the Bill came before the House of Commons, to the arguments put forward. There was a suggestion that somehow or other it was based upon a game of skill. I cannot help but think that anyone who would believe that is naive in the extreme. There is no game of skill involved; it is a game of chance. It is just like any other game of chance.
June 29, 1983

One has an option and picks between teams or among teams a combination of victors and losers, the end result of which is that one's chance at winning is so remote that one might as well give away the money to the first poor person on the street. That would do more good than going through this process which the Government has established.
I want to make it absolutely clear that we are unalterably opposed to the passage of this Bill. We were opposed to it at second reading. I went into some detail at second reading as to why I felt it was inappropriate. In fact, with a little bit of humour I dealt with my then recent visit to Las Vegas. 1 had taken my son to Las Vegas just to see the place. At that time 1 pointed out the despair that I saw on the faces of those who walked out of the gambling casinos, the haggard faces of the gamblers who had sat there-

I lost absolutely nothing. I never bet, as you know. I saw the haggard and unshaven faces of those who became hooked on the slot machines and the blackjack and poker tables that were there.
Over the years concern has been expressed to me by the families of those who have become addicts. Just as people become addicted to drugs and alcohol, they become addicted to gambling. They become addicted in such a way that the income from their job becomes insufficient to meet their addiction. Family homes are lost because of this as well as the family incomes which are necessary to provide for their day to day well-being.
While I do not pretend for one moment that the purchase of a lottery ticket will necessarily make that financial and substantial difference, I do not believe that the Government should be in the business of promoting further gambling.

Including the Government of Manitoba; I do not make any distinctions. When 1 am opposed to something, I am opposed regardless of who does it. I will be blunt here; 1 was opposed when the Government of Ontario brought in Win-tario. I said so in the Legislature. I might say that I was in the minority, but 1 stood and said that I was opposed to it, that it was wrong and it was not the direction to go. I would say the same to any government, regardless of its political leaning, that that is not the appropriate direction to go.
If we want to fund something like the Olympics, if a decision is made after careful consideration that it is important for Canada to host the Olympics or some other major sporting event, we then take on the concurrent responsibility to raise the money through normal channels to ensure that the funding is available.
What worries me about all of this is that we are looking at a set amount of money. I hope it is a set amount of money. There are just so many dollars available for the purchase of lottery tickets. All kinds of lotteries are being conducted from coast to coast. If we add a new lottery to the existing myriad of
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
lotteries, we just further distribute the money. It is not new money. Other lotteries which supposedly provide money for local events, such as amateur baseball, amateur hockey, and in the case of Ontario and some other Provinces medical research, no doubt worth-while purposes, there will be fewer dollars available to those institutions as a result of our entering the field.
The end result will be that amateur hockey, baseball, lacrosse, and charitable organizations that attempt to provide recreation in many communities in this country will find that there are fewer dollars available to them; therefore they will not be able to meet their commitments. Children in every part of this country will not have the same degree of access that they have had in the past.
From my point of view, it seems to fly in the face of everything we believe in. I do not often use this kind of term, but frankly, I consider this to be morally wrong. It is wrong to be in the business in the first place. From a practical point of view, I also consider it to be wrong. It takes away from existing charitable funding that is so necessary in many communities. In many ways it is a further enticement to those who can ill afford it. They use the few dollars they have in the fond hope of that elusive prize, a prize which escapes almost all of them.
I urge the Government that it consider these arguments. I understand that they are not powerful arguments and that they have been made before; they are really just a response from my own experience with this. If it is the desire of the Government to fund whatever major undertakings we deem necessary for the enchancement of Canada's way of life and the enhancement of Canada on the international scene, we should do that legitimately. There are various means available to us now through the existing tax structure and the appeal for donations which are tax deductible and, therefore, beneficial to those who can afford to make them. However, we should not add further to the ongoing problems that develop as a result of encouraging people to believe that somewhere at the end of all this there is a pot of gold that they can reach for and thereby get something for nothing. You get nothing for nothing. Lotteries tend to sell on the basis of that theme. You do not get anything in this world without putting some effort into it. You will not become rich quickly from the purchase of a lottery ticket.
If people want to make contributions to the ongoing events of Canada, whatever they may be, they should do so according to their ability and their desire. Surely it should not be on the basis of the hope that they will derive some financial reward in the end, that they will become fabulously wealthy, because that financial reward eludes all but a few. The financial reward causes suffering even to those who win.
Even at this late point 1 urge the Government to reconsider and to agree that what it is proposing is not appropriate. To suggest that somehow or other it will enhance the sporting events of this land is ludicrous. The proper way to build a society is through a fair and equitable means of raising money,

not through a get-rich-quick scheme based on the sale of lottery tickets.

Mr. Speaker,
1 was going to begin by commending the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) for the sincerity of his remarks because he certainly expressed many views that have been expressed by Members of this Party, although rather infrequently by some Members of his own Party, during the course of the previous debate. In light of the question asked by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), I am not quite as assured of the sincerity of the Party which the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain represents, but nonetheless, his response seemed to be sincere in that he adheres to his position, which is, as I understand it, that governments in the country should not be participating in the gaming rackets.
As has been very capably expressed by many of my colleagues and especially by our spokesman in this debate, the Hon. I would like to say that I think it sets a very poor example when Members of the Crown, those who are appointed to take charge and accept
responsibility for the major problems in our society, which are principally unemployment and inflation, the management of Government and the maintenance of respect for law and order, set such a retrograde standard for all Canadians to witness.
This is particularly true, Mr. Speaker, in terms of the example set by for young people by the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan), who is pushing this Bill through the House on behalf of his colleague in the other place. Our young people are hopefully being brought up in a society which establishes law and allows people to pursue their own adventures at their own risks, but society must set certain standards for the people of the country to follow. I would like to assert again that I believe this Minister and the Government are helping to contribute to the degradation of the values that many of us in the country hold dear.
The valuable time of Ministers of the Crown is being taken to participate in the kind of gambling that we do not allow many other groups in the country to participate in. We are rigorous in terms of %ur enforcement of laws with regard to off-track betting. We regularly instruct the RCMP to raid the gambling houses of many Chinese Canadians who for centuries have participated in their traditional games of chance. Yet under the Criminal Code those games of chance are outlawed and people participating in them are prosecuted to the full limit of the law. I think that it is reprehensible when the Government comes to the House with a piece of legislation which would amend the Criminal Code to suit its convenience while it continues to prosecute people who operate games of chance without its sanction.
I do not know what the current practice is, but in fact, in the past charitable organizations that have run various types of raffles and lotteries and bingo games for various good works in the community have been punished and treated virtually as criminals by this Government and many of its predecessors. Yet now it is setting a new standard for our society.
The stated purpose of the Bill, Mr. Speaker, is to raise funds for so-called good works in our nation. It is to provide financial assistance for fitness and amateur sports, arts and culture, and medical and health research, as is stated in the list that is contained in Clause 18 of the Bill. Finally, and low on the list, comes the provision of funding for the Calgary Olympics.
The people of Canada are being told by Liberal Party Members and all of their paid publicity backs that we on this side of the House are holding up this Bill and therefore jeopardizing the conduct of the Calgary Olympics. Yet this Bill does not even establish a priority in terms of access to available funding for the Calgary Olympics. It puts it as the last item on the list. The Government has refused to accept our second amendment to this legislation which would make the Calgary Olympics the sole beneficiary of this initiative. I think, Mr. Speaker, that that belies the credibility of the Government's pronouncements outside this House that the poor people of Calgary and western Canada will not get the same kind of treatment that Montreal did in terms of the previous Olympics
June 29, 1983

if Conservative Members keep digging in their heels and opposing the Bill.
The fact of the matter, Mr. Speaker, is that we believe the Calgary Olympics can be funded and that the federal Government has a responsibility to share in the cost of those games, but there are various ways of financing such initiatives. The best and most direct means of doing so in the case of something as important and prestigious to Calgary and all of Canada as the Olympics would be to introduce a tax credit system that is the same as the one that operates in the financing of political parties in the country.
The Government could have allowed a 75 per cent tax credit on all contributions up to $200 from Canadians at large who would contribute to the Calgary Olympics. Then we would not have had to award patronage to all friends of the Liberal Party who want to build computer machines and earn commissions and set up stands in shopping centres. We would not have had to spend all of that money on advertising. We would not have had to con the Canadian people into thinking that they can get rich quick, therefore setting a standard of moral corruption on the part of the Government which runs in total contradiction to all of the progressive measures of taxation legislation that this Government and many of its predecessors have established over the years.
By a mere admendment to the Income Tax Act, the Government could attract millions of dollars for the Calgary Olympics and other worthy causes. This simple amendment would make it possible for people who contribute to charity to opt between sending a significant portion of their dollars to Ottawa or to some worthy cause. I guarantee that this would eliminate a whole layer of unnecessary bureaucracy here in Ottawa. It would allow Cabinet Ministers to take charge again of the important tasks for which they are responsible instead of wasting their energies on such corruption as a sports lottery.
I believe the Minister should hand his head in shame because, in fact, what he is doing runs totally contrary to the whole thrust and intent of the Family Allowance system, the Child Tax Credit system, our federal-provincial agreements on welfare payments, the Unemployment Insurance system, the old age pension system, the guaranteed annual income system for those in need, and all of our social support systems, Mr. Speaker. In particular, the very progressive nature of our income tax structure as represented in the tax table is being contravened by this measure that will get the Government of Canada back into the lottery business. We reject this initiative without equivocation even though, as the Hon. Member for St. Catharines pointed out, we cannot go on obstructing all summer. If this is the Government's only way, in its obstinan-cy, to see to it that the people of western Canada are not left carrying the can for the Calgary Olympics, then I suppose we will have to let the measure go through.
Mark my words, Mr. Speaker, just as Loto Canada failed, just as Loto Select failed even before it got off the ground after the Government wasted $37 million on that boondoggle, this sports pool corporation will also fail. My colleague has wished
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
it well, but if I have anything to say in the next Government of Canada, I will ensure that this type of corrupt initiative is replaced with proper and progressive amendments to the Income Tax Act. We must ensure that volunteer organizations are again funded by Canadians giving of their own free will and not by those who want to get rich quick by taking a chance on a lottery ticket.
In the course of the debate many statistics have been produced to show that those who buy lottery tickets are people at the low end of the income scale. The Minister shakes his head but he knows full well that those who are most careful with their money, the shrewd investors in society, the successes in society, do not buy lottery tickets. He knows that it is the people who get a welfare cheque who buy lottery tickets. They think they have a chance because they see on television or read about some elderly couple who won a million dollars and so they tend to feel that they too have chance, even though the odds are something like 10 million to one against their winning. The odds against happiness after winning are great as well. Nonetheless, the Government is enticing people who can least afford it to buy tickets. Every time they walk into a shopping mall or go to a sporting even or turn on the television, they are coerced and persuaded by the Government of Canada, with that nice, neat, official Liberal logo, to buy lottery tickets. That reflects the moral bankruptcy and corruption of this Government.
When we couple this move with the introduction of electronics into gaming and see the potential for abuse-for outright fraud by people who know how to write computer programs- and when we connect that with some of the people who will be licensed to sell tickets, we see the potential for harm. The concessionaires with license to sell the tickets are usually good friends of the Liberal Party. When we couple that with the people who get the contract to build the systems, like a constituent of mine who is looking for the contract to build these systems and happens to be a former Liberal Cabinet Minister by the name of Cafik, we see the potential for abuse if there is no requirement for public accountability.
I suggest there is the possibility of a major scam being perpetrated, not in the Government's official name, but by people who would stoop to that. The system can be rigged, Mr. Speaker. We have not been convinced that there will be control over the issuance of vouchers. Anyone can program a computer to spew out a lot of extra tickets. There will be no control on the odds; they will just keep selling tickets because they want to raise money for worthy causes.
If the wrong people intervene in the system-and here we are getting into the area of computer crime-a lot of money can be siphoned out of the system. That is why one of the amendments put forward by this Party asked that the books and accounts of the Sports Canada Corporation should be fully audited and scrutinized by the Auditor General. We find it strange that the Government rejected that amendment, just as it rejected our amendment to ensure that the funds would go first to the Calgary Olympics. The Government also rejected

June 29, 1983
our amendment which would have assured that this move could not lead to a wide open promotion of a myriad of electronic games. We are already plagued with these in our communities. Our kids are hanging out at the electronic pinball palaces, where they run into people who push drugs and commit petty break and entry in order to pay for their habit. We read about that in society today.
The Government has rejected our amendment which would have restricted the scope of this kind of lottery, so there is nothing to prevent it from going into all kinds of electronic gaming and distributing these things in our communities where they can corrupt our children. This can all be done with the nice red and white Liberal Party logo stamped in the corner- "officially on behalf of the Government of Canada".
I think that what the Minister is trying to put over in the House smells to high heaven, Mr. Speaker. I put a question in the House to the former Minister who had responsibility for Loto Select. That boondoggle had ordered $17,000 worth of foil-wrapped chocolate candies to be given away as a promotional gimmick. It had leased space in a building in Vancouver, hired a lot of people and entered into a contract with General Instruments of the United States, without going to tender, for
2,000	slot machines as part of the Loto Select initiative. At the end, the whole thing was written off at a cost of $37 million, including severance allowances and $10,000 compensation for over 50 employees.
This all happened under the aegis of that other great prominent Liberal, the former Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sports who came from Skeena and who now presents herself as President of the Liberal Party of Canada and perhaps future candidate for the leadership of that Party. In answer to the question I put to her in December, 1978 about the corruption, scandal and lack of control over the Loto Select boondoggle, she said that Canadian lottery winners are extremely intelligent in their investment in Loto Canada because they are able to maintain most of their dollars in their bank accounts.
Such stupidity, Mr. Speaker; such utter, unadulterated stupidity. This was the reply of a Minister of the Crown who was giving all her time to promoting Loto Canada. She was running around smiling, jumping over barricades and pretending to be a fitness freak when she should have been attending to Government business in some important economic portfolio. We are going around in that same old circle again, Mr. Speaker, with the present Minister who is not destined to sit long in this House. But he wants to go out in flames of glory and leave something that we will have to eliminate when we take office.
The former Minister said that Canadian lottery winners are extremely intelligent in their investment because they are able to maintain most of their dollars in their bank accounts. What about the losers, Mr. Speaker? The losers are the ten million who buy a ticket and do not win. What about the investment in
their bank account? They are spending household money at the rate of $40 per capita. If we were to examine the weighting toward low-income Canadians, I wager that many of them would be spending $100 per capita. What about their bank accounts? Is it so intelligent for the Government to encourage them to spend money that should be spent on children's shoes and clothing, mortgage payments and all the things they need in times of tremendous economic difficulty? It smells of moral bankruptcy, Mr. Speaker.
It is quite clear that Members of this Party will vote against this measure. All the indications are that the revenues predicted cannot possibly be realized. If the Quebec hockey lottery is any example, the Government will be lucky to raise $10 million or $20 million, not the $80 million or $100 million that was predicted.
In conclusion, I should like to say that the people of Canada will remember this and demand some changes. Already they are demanding a return to family values and respect for all the things that government should do as an example to our children. I for one will do everything I can to eliminate the sports pool operation when it comes before the next Government of Canada.
